summary: Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity provider: it stores users, groups, devices, and application identities, and issues the tokens every sign-in depends on. Privileged Identity Management (PIM) converts standing (always-on) privileged access into eligible, just-in-time access, while Conditional Access (CA) evaluates risk and context signals after the first authentication factor to decide whether to grant, block, or add friction to a sign-in. Authentication methods policy and Authentication strength push the tenant toward phishing-resistant, passwordless sign-in.
keyPoints: PIM distinguishes **eligible** (allowed to activate, not yet usable) from **active** (currently usable, either standing or a time-bound post-activation window). Without PIM, an admin holds their role as permanent standing access. PIM requires Microsoft Entra ID P2.
PIM governs Microsoft Entra directory roles (Global Administrator, Security Administrator), Azure resource roles (Owner, Contributor), and privileged access groups — not just one system.

Configure eligibility: Entra admin center ▸ Identity Governance ▸ Privileged Identity Management ▸ Microsoft Entra roles ▸ Roles ▸ select the role ▸ Add assignments ▸ Eligible, with an optional end date. Role settings control maximum activation duration, require MFA, require justification, and require approval (naming approvers).

Activation: PIM ▸ My roles ▸ Eligible assignments ▸ Activate, subject to whatever gates the role's settings define, producing a time-bound active assignment. PIM access reviews recertify eligible/active assignments periodically, and built-in alerts flag risks like 'too many Global Administrators' or 'administrators not using PIM'.

Conditional Access is a policy engine evaluated **after** the first factor (e.g., password) succeeds — it is not a perimeter or anti-DoS control. Assignments define the 'if': users/groups/roles, workload identities, target resources (cloud apps / all resources, user actions), and conditions (sign-in risk, user risk, platform, location/IP, client app, device filters).

Access controls define the 'then': Grant controls (block, or allow with MFA / compliant device / hybrid-joined device / approved client app / password change / terms of use) and Session controls (sign-in frequency, persistent browser session, app-enforced restrictions, Conditional Access App Control). Authentication strength lets a policy require a specific method set, such as phishing-resistant MFA only.

Licensing: **P1** is the minimum for Conditional Access. **P2** adds Microsoft Entra ID Protection (risk-based CA using sign-in risk and user risk) and PIM. **SSPR** lets users reset their own password. **TAP** (Temporary Access Pass) is a time-limited passcode used to bootstrap registration of passwordless methods.

Roll-out pattern for a new CA policy: build it in **Report-only**, validate the intended effect in sign-in logs, then switch it **On**. Always exclude break-glass accounts from both CA and PIM so a misconfiguration or outage can never lock out every administrator.

Conditional Access does not evaluate service principals authenticating with client credentials under user-targeted policies — Conditional Access for workload identities is the dedicated mechanism for daemons and automation. Legacy authentication (which cannot satisfy MFA prompts) must be blocked with its own policy.

Passwordless methods — Windows Hello for Business (biometric/PIN bound to a TPM), FIDO2 security keys/passkeys, and Microsoft Authenticator phone sign-in — are managed in the Authentication methods policy. Microsoft's preferred order is phishing-resistant methods, then Authenticator push with number matching, then OATH/TOTP, then SMS/voice (weakest, vulnerable to SIM-swap).
commonPitfalls: Treating 'eligible' as if it already grants access — the principal must still activate the role, subject to any configured MFA/justification/approval gates.
Confusing Report-only with Off — Report-only evaluates and logs the policy's would-be effect without enforcing grant or block controls.
Forgetting to exclude break-glass accounts from Conditional Access and PIM, risking a full administrative lockout if a policy misfires or MFA is unavailable.

Assuming a user-targeted Conditional Access policy also protects daemons and service principals authenticating with client credentials — it does not; use Conditional Access for workload identities instead.

Treating SMS or voice-call verification as strong MFA — they are the weakest factors and are vulnerable to SIM-swap attacks; phishing-resistant methods (FIDO2, Windows Hello) are the recommended target.
Skipping periodic PIM access reviews, letting stale eligible assignments and unused standing access accumulate unnoticed.

Assign an Azure resource role directly with Azure CLI, for contrast with a PIM eligible assignment
commands.cli: az role assignment create --assignee user@contoso.com --role Contributor --scope /subscriptions/<subId>

summary: Registering an application in Microsoft Entra ID creates two linked objects: an app registration (the global blueprint, defining redirect URIs, secrets/certificates, and requested API permissions) and, in every tenant that uses the app, a service principal managed under Enterprise applications (the local, governable instance that actually receives permissions, sign-in policy, and consent). Managed identities are a special category of service principal whose credentials Azure creates and rotates automatically, eliminating stored secrets entirely.
keyPoints: **App registration** defines what the app is and can request — redirect URIs, certificates & secrets, and requested API permissions. One app registration produces one **service principal per tenant** that consumes it (a multi-tenant app gets a distinct service principal in every consuming tenant).

**Enterprise application** is where you govern that service principal locally — assign users/groups, enable SSO, apply Conditional Access, and review the OAuth permission **grants** actually consented to (as opposed to only requested on the app registration).
**Delegated permissions** act on behalf of a signed-in user and are bounded by what that user could do themselves; depending on policy, consent can come from the user or an administrator.

**Application permissions** act as the app itself with no signed-in user present (daemons, background jobs), are often high-privilege, and **always** require admin consent — granted tenant-wide, not per user.

Manage tenant-wide consent under Enterprise applications ▸ Consent and permissions: restrict **user consent** to verified publishers and low-impact permissions (or disable it), and enable the **admin consent workflow** so requests route to named reviewers — this closes the door on illicit consent grant attacks.

**Managed identities** give an Azure resource (VM, Function App, Logic App, AKS, etc.) its own Entra identity with Azure-rotated credentials — there is no client secret or certificate to store, leak, or rotate manually.

**System-assigned** managed identity: created with, and deleted alongside, a single host resource — a strict 1:1 relationship, ideal for one workload. **User-assigned** managed identity: a standalone Azure resource that can be attached to multiple resources and survives independently — ideal for a shared identity across a fleet.

To let a VM read a Key Vault secret without any stored credential: enable a managed identity on the VM, then grant that identity the **Key Vault Secrets User** role (or an equivalent access policy) on the vault.

Preference order for workload authentication: **managed identity** > service principal with **certificate** > service principal with **client secret** — always prefer the option furthest left that the workload supports.

Periodically review Enterprise applications ▸ Permissions to find and remove unused high-privilege application-permission grants (e.g., an unused Mail.ReadWrite application permission), since application permissions carry outsized risk with no user context to limit blast radius.
commonPitfalls: Swapping app registration (blueprint / what's requested) and enterprise application (local governed instance / what's actually granted) — a frequent source of exam distractors.
Assuming a narrowly-named application permission is automatically low-risk — application permissions always require admin consent and always act without user context.
Forgetting that admin consent is granted **tenant-wide**, not per user — approving a request opens the permission for every user in the tenant.
Reaching for a service principal with a client secret when the workload already runs on an Azure resource capable of hosting a managed identity.
Believing a system-assigned managed identity can be shared across resources — only user-assigned identities can be attached to more than one resource.

commands.task: Enable a system-assigned managed identity on an existing VM
commands.cli: az vm identity assign --name VM1 --resource-group RG1

summary: Azure Key Vault centralizes three object types — keys, secrets, and certificates — behind two possible authorization models and an independent network layer. Azure RBAC is the recommended, centrally governed model; vault access policies are a legacy, vault-scoped alternative. Defender for Key Vault and Defender CSPM secret scanning are complementary but distinct: one watches the vault at runtime, the other hunts for secrets exposed elsewhere.
keyPoints: Key Vault stores **keys** (cryptographic keys for encrypt/sign operations, optionally HSM-backed), **secrets** (passwords, connection strings, tokens), and **certificates** (X.509, with auto-renewal via integrated certificate authorities).

**Managed HSM** is a separate, single-tenant, FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated offering for organizations needing dedicated HSM isolation — distinct from **Premium-tier** HSM-protected keys inside a normal, shared vault.

**Azure RBAC (recommended)**: built-in roles (Key Vault Secrets User, Key Vault Administrator, etc.) assigned at any scope — management group, subscription, resource group, or vault — centrally consistent with the rest of Azure RBAC and compatible with PIM.

**Vault access policy (legacy)**: per-principal, per-object-type operation lists (get/list/set/...) configurable only at the vault level — simpler to reason about locally, but not centrally governed and not PIM-eligible.

Network restriction (Public network access **Disabled** + private endpoint, or a firewall scoped to specific VNets/IPs) governs reachability, but authorization (RBAC or access policy) is enforced **independently and in addition** — both gates must pass for a request to succeed.

**Allow trusted Microsoft services to bypass this firewall** lets first-party integrations like Azure Backup or Azure Disk Encryption reach a network-restricted vault; omitting it breaks those integrations.

**Defender for Key Vault** (a paid Defender for Cloud plan) is runtime, data-plane threat detection on the vault: alerts on anomalous access such as unusual identities, unusually high volume, or connections from Tor exit nodes.

**Defender CSPM secret scanning** is a separate, agentless posture capability that discovers plaintext secrets sitting outside the vault — on disks, in source code, or in environment variables — and maps the attack path to sensitive resources; it does not watch the vault's runtime traffic.

**Customer-managed keys (CMK)** stored in Key Vault let you control encryption for services like storage accounts, managed disks, and SQL TDE. **Bring Your Own Key (BYOK)** imports a key generated or held outside Azure into Key Vault (or Managed HSM) to use as that CMK.

**Soft-delete** (on by default, 7-90 day retention) and **purge protection** together prevent accidental or malicious permanent deletion of vaults or their objects before the retention window elapses.

**Automated key rotation**: a rotation policy on a key (time-based, or before a configured expiry threshold) creates new key versions automatically with no manual intervention — apps that reference the key by name (latest version) pick up the rotated version transparently, shrinking the window a compromised key stays usable.

**Zero-downtime secret rotation** uses a **dual-credential pattern**: create the new secret version while the old version is still valid, update consumers to the new version, then retire the old one — rotating a secret **in place** (overwriting the only version) creates an outage window for any consumer that hasn't yet picked up the new value.

Key Vault integrates with **Azure Event Grid** to react to lifecycle events (e.g. a certificate nearing expiry, a new secret version created) in near real time — commonly used to trigger a Logic App that renews a certificate or notifies an owner automatically.

**Diagnostic logging** sends Key Vault operation logs (the `AuditEvent` category) to a Log Analytics workspace, storage account, or Event Hub; **log-based alert rules** can then fire on suspicious patterns such as high-volume secret retrieval — this is separate from, and complements, Defender for Key Vault's built-in runtime alerts.
commonPitfalls: Assuming a locked-down vault firewall is enough on its own — RBAC or access-policy authorization is still enforced on top, and both checks must pass.
Forgetting 'Allow trusted Microsoft services' when restricting the firewall, silently breaking Azure Backup or Azure Disk Encryption integrations.
Confusing Defender for Key Vault (runtime threat detection **on** the vault) with Defender CSPM secret scanning (finding secrets exposed **elsewhere**) — they answer different questions.
Defaulting new vaults to legacy vault access policies instead of the centrally governed, PIM-compatible RBAC model.
Leaving purge protection disabled, which allows a soft-deleted vault or object to be purged permanently before the recovery window would otherwise protect it.

Relying on a manual, calendar-reminder rotation instead of configuring an automated rotation policy — a missed manual rotation silently extends how long a potentially compromised key or secret stays valid.

Rotating a secret in place (a single version, overwritten) instead of using the dual-credential pattern, causing an outage for any consumer that hasn't yet picked up the new value before the old one disappears.

commands.task: Create a Key Vault with RBAC authorization, soft-delete, and purge protection
commands.cli: az keyvault create --name kv-tailspin --resource-group RG1 --location eastus --enable-rbac-authorization true --enable-purge-protection true

commands.task: Grant a managed identity read access to secrets via an RBAC role
commands.cli: az role assignment create --assignee <principalId> --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --scope /subscriptions/<subId>/resourceGroups/RG1/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/kv-tailspin

commands.task: Disable public network access while allowing trusted Microsoft services
commands.cli: az keyvault update --name kv-tailspin --resource-group RG1 --public-network-access Disabled --bypass AzureServices

commands.task: Create a private endpoint for the vault
commands.cli: az network private-endpoint create --name kv-pe --resource-group RG1 --vnet-name VNet1 --subnet snet-pe --private-connection-resource-id /subscriptions/<subId>/resourceGroups/RG1/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/kv-tailspin --group-id vault --connection-name kv-connection

summary: Azure Policy governs the properties a resource is allowed to have, while Azure RBAC governs the actions a principal may perform — two complementary but distinct control planes. On top of that, resource locks, Azure Backup hardening, regulatory compliance mapping, and pre-deployment Infrastructure as Code scanning round out the governance layer that keeps an environment compliant and resilient against both misconfiguration and compromised administrators.
keyPoints: Azure Policy evaluates resources against rule definitions and reports or enforces compliance. Unlike RBAC (what a principal **can do**), Policy governs what properties a resource **can have**.

Effects: **Audit** (logs non-compliance, still allows it), **Deny** (blocks non-compliant create/update), **DeployIfNotExists/DINE** (auto-remediates via a deployment, e.g. enabling diagnostics — requires a managed identity on the assignment), **Modify** (adds/changes properties or tags), **AuditIfNotExists** (flags when a related resource is missing).

Related definitions are bundled into **initiatives** (e.g. the built-in Microsoft cloud security benchmark) and assigned as a set at management group, subscription, or resource group scope. Custom definitions are JSON with a `policyRule` if/then block and parameters.

DINE and Modify assignments only affect resources going forward; bringing existing non-compliant resources into line requires running a **remediation task**, which uses the managed identity created for the policy assignment.

Azure RBAC and Microsoft Entra roles are **two separate systems**: Azure RBAC governs resources (subscriptions, VMs, storage) via principal + role definition + scope, with permissions inheriting downward; Microsoft Entra roles govern the directory (users, groups, app registrations). Global Administrator is an Entra role; Owner is an Azure role — neither grants the other.

Built-in Azure roles: **Owner** (full access, including granting access to others), **Contributor** (manages resources but cannot grant access), **Reader** (read-only), **User Access Administrator** (manages role assignments but not the resources themselves). Custom roles in either system use their own JSON shape — Azure custom roles use `Actions`/`NotActions`/`DataActions`/`NotDataActions`/`AssignableScopes`.

**Resource locks**: `CanNotDelete` (read/modify allowed, delete blocked) and `ReadOnly` (no modify, no delete). Locks apply **independently of RBAC** — even an Owner is blocked by an active lock — and are inherited by child resources.

**Azure Backup hardening**: soft-delete (recover deleted backup data for a window, roughly 14 days, and can be made always-on), **immutable vaults** (backup data's retention cannot be shortened or the data deleted during the retention period), and **Multi-User Authorization (MUA)** via a **Resource Guard** — a second, separately-permissioned administrator must approve destructive operations (disabling soft-delete, deleting backup data), defending against both ransomware and a rogue or compromised administrator.

Defender for Cloud's **Regulatory compliance** dashboard maps the environment against frameworks (Microsoft cloud security benchmark by default, plus PCI-DSS, ISO 27001, NIST, CIS) and tracks pass/fail controls; standards are added or removed under Environment settings ▸ Security policy.

**Infrastructure as Code security** means scanning Bicep/ARM/Terraform templates **before** deployment for misconfigurations (public storage, missing encryption) — 'shift left'. Defender for Cloud's **DevOps security** connects to GitHub/Azure DevOps to surface IaC scan findings and secrets exposed in repositories. The **Microsoft DevOps (MSDO) extension** is the specific Azure DevOps/GitHub Actions extension that runs this IaC and secret scanning as part of a pipeline, feeding results back into Defender for Cloud's DevOps security and a policy-as-code workflow.

**Governance rules** in Defender for Cloud assign **ownership** of a security recommendation to a specific person or team, with a due date and email notifications — driving accountability so recommendations don't sit unassigned indefinitely.

For a control that legitimately doesn't apply to a given resource, Defender for Cloud supports a structured, documented, time-bound **exemption** at the recommendation or policy level — distinct from the one-click **Fix** action, which applies an available automated remediation directly to a non-compliant resource.
commonPitfalls: Treating Policy and RBAC as interchangeable — Policy governs resource properties/compliance, RBAC governs what a principal can do.

Assigning a DINE or Modify policy and assuming existing resources are automatically fixed — they require a remediation task using the assignment's managed identity; only new/updated resources are covered immediately.
Assuming a Global Administrator automatically has Owner on Azure resources (or vice versa) — the two role systems never cross-grant.
Believing a resource lock is a substitute for RBAC — locks block delete/modify regardless of RBAC permissions, but say nothing about who can read or grant access.

Relying on soft-delete alone for backup protection when Multi-User Authorization (Resource Guard) isn't configured, leaving a single compromised admin able to disable soft-delete or shorten retention.
Scanning Infrastructure as Code only after deployment instead of pre-deployment, missing the opportunity to block a misconfiguration before it is ever provisioned.
Leaving security recommendations unassigned instead of using governance rules to name an owner and due date — unassigned recommendations tend to stay unresolved indefinitely.

Confusing an **exemption** (a documented, time-bound waiver for a control that legitimately doesn't apply) with **Fix** (a one-click action that actually remediates a non-compliant resource) — they solve opposite problems.
